en: Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, and Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing and others, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
the Buddha then addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: "Subhūti!
Form has no-nature, conventional nature, and real nature;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no-nature, conventional nature, and real nature. Subhūti!

In this way, it extends even to the eye, forms, and visual consciousness; the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness; the nose, odors, and olfactory consciousness; the tongue, tastes, and gustatory consciousness; the body, tangibles, and tactile consciousness; and the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness—all of which lack intrinsic nature, possess a provisional nature, and possess a real nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Form evolves within these three natures; that which the ignorant practice, one should know to be the correct practice of a bodhisattva."
A practitioner who acts in this way will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands the dharma of signlessness within all consciousnesses, suffering ceases of its own accord and all signs become tranquil.
One should know that such practice is the correct practice of a bodhisattva.
"A practitioner who acts in this way will swiftly realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If one understands the dharma of signlessness, All sufferings will naturally cease."
All marks are utterly tranquil; this is the practice of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, among all forms, darkness and light equally depend upon one another.
If a bodhisattva can understand this as it truly is and enter into it through comprehension, all phenomena are likewise so.
Such a bodhisattva will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within all forms of consciousness, darkness and light equally depend upon one another.”
If a bodhisattva can understand this as it truly is and enter into it through comprehension, all phenomena are likewise so.
Such a bodhisattva will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“If phenomena are both dark and bright, such is their nature of equality;
by relying upon and penetrating this understanding, one realizes awakening once it is known.”

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all forms, Subhūti, and regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, turns away from the three natures—if a wise person understands this as it truly is, they will not give rise to grasping or attachment within consciousness, nor will they manifest such turning; their mind becomes clear and luminous."

Because they do not give rise to grasping or attachment toward consciousness and their minds have become clear and enlightened, they are able to achieve liberation within the Mahāyāna teachings, let alone within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas!

Furthermore, because they do not give rise to grasping or attachment in this way and their minds are opened and clarified, they will not undergo the suffering of birth and death for a long time within those various realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Is form produced? Or is it extinguished?"
If one says that form has arising, that form is itself non-arising;
if one says that form is non-arising, that form is itself the self-nature of non-arising.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva understands according to reality that form is itself the self-nature of non-arising, therefore, regarding form, there can be no arising.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Is consciousness produced?”
Is it for the sake of extinguishing [the view of] annihilation? If one says that consciousness has arising, that consciousness is itself non-arising;
if one says that consciousness has no arising, that consciousness is the very nature of non-arising.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva understands as it truly is that consciousness is itself the nature of non-arising, then for that reason, no arising of consciousness can occur. "Moreover, Subhūti!"
If someone should say,
"Form is my self, it belongs to me," I declare that such a person is the most external among the external, a foolish worldling in a state of wrong view.
“Subhūti! If someone were to say:
‘Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self, they are mine.’”
“Whoever speaks thus, I declare them to be the most external among the external, foolish commoners abiding in the state of wrong views. Furthermore, Subhūti!”
If someone were to say:
"Form is produced by causes established in previous lives;
or it is produced by the creative agency of Maheśvara."
"Or that there are no causes and conditions.
To those who speak thus, I say they are the most extreme among outsiders, foolish ordinary beings in a state of wrong view. "Subhūti!..."
If someone should say:
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are produced by causes established in a previous life;
or they are produced by the creative agency of Maheśvara."
"Or that there are no causes and conditions.
To those who speak thus, I say they are the most extreme among outsiders, foolish worldlings in a state of wrong view.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If someone were to say: "Form has the characteristic of form-image; sensation has the characteristic of experiencing; perception has the characteristic of full cognition; formations have the characteristic of volitional activity; and consciousness has the characteristic of discernment."
“Whoever speaks thus, I declare them to be the most external among the external, foolish worldlings in a state of wrong view. Furthermore, Subhūti!”
If someone were to say:
"Suffering is not tranquil;
if that form ceases, this pleasure becomes tranquil."
"One who speaks thus, I declare, is the most external among the external, a foolish worldling in the state of wrong views.
Subhūti, if someone should say: "
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus: they are suffering and not tranquil;
if that consciousness ceases, this pleasure is tranquil.
To speak in this way, I say that such a person is the most external of the external, a foolish worldling in the state of wrong view.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If someone were to say:
'That form is non-existent;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also all non-existent. "
"One who speaks thus, I declare, is the most external among the external—the foolish commoner abiding in the state of wrong views. Furthermore, Subhūti:
If someone were to say:
"As the Buddha has taught:
'Form has no intrinsic nature; it is neither born nor extinguished; it is originally quiescent and by its very nature in nirvāṇa.'"

"One who speaks thus—regarding all phenomena, they neither find harmony nor have any aspiration for them, yet they form such a conceptual understanding based on their own words—I declare that such a person is the most extreme among outsiders, a foolish worldling in the state of wrong views."
“Subhūti! If someone were to say:

‘Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this; as the Buddha has taught, they all lack intrinsic nature, are neither arising nor ceasing, are originally quiescent, and are by nature nirvāṇa.’”

Regarding those who speak thus—they have neither integration nor aspiration toward any phenomena, yet they form such understandings according to their own verbal expressions—I declare them to be the most extreme among outsiders, foolish worldlings in a state of false views.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there is another person who conceives of form as existing, grasps at form, and gives rise to [notions] regarding it, turning according to verbal expression;
and furthermore, conceiving of form as existing, they rely upon that very form for defilement, turning according to the presence of signs; [this is so]."
Furthermore, one reckons form as existing and cultivates pure dharmas toward that very form, thereby establishing its conformity.
"Subhūti, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Furthermore, if there is someone who reckons consciousness to exist, who grasps at consciousness as something that arises, and who revolves according to verbal expressions;
or again, if they reckon consciousness to exist, they then rely upon that very consciousness for defilement, and revolve with its signs.
Furthermore, they reckon consciousness to exist; they cultivate pure dharmas within that very consciousness and establish its subsequent transformation.

"Moreover, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas reckon form to exist, they perceive cessation and knowledge within that form, and they accomplish verbal expressions regarding the practice of great bliss, thereby following its transformation."
Furthermore, bodhisattvas conceive of form as existent; regarding that form, they have cessation and knowledge, they express and accomplish it, and they proceed accordingly with whatever arises.

Moreover, bodhisattvas conceive of form as existent; within that form, by means of their ability to fully understand the perfection of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), and having attained mastery over all phenomena, they are able to proceed in accordance with the practice of great bliss.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If bodhisattvas reckon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to be existent, they will perceive cessation and cognition within that consciousness, and they will engage in the discourse and accomplishment of the practice of great bliss, following along with whatever arises.”

Furthermore, bodhisattvas conceive of consciousness as existent; within that consciousness, they possess cessation and cognition, manifesting accomplishment and evolving accordingly. Moreover, bodhisattvas conceive of consciousness as existent;

within that consciousness, they are able to fully comprehend the perfection of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), meaning that having attained mastery over all phenomena, they are able to evolve in accordance with the practice of great bliss.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there is another person who cannot, regarding form, observe with reality and equanimity the measure of form within form, or the measure of suffering within suffering, then they have a grasping for a self within form;
if they have a grasping for a self within form, then they have a grasping for the view of a self within form."
If one perceives a view of self within form, one perceives a view of sentient beings within form;
if one perceives a view of sentient beings within form, one finds no such view of sentient beings within form;
and when one finds no view of sentient beings within form, then those sentient beings themselves are also not found.

If there were any characteristic of attainment regarding phenomena that could be established, then that characteristic of attainment would have a basis; consequently, one would be unable to achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.

If there is someone who, regarding consciousness, perceives its measure, and regarding suffering, perceives its measure, yet cannot contemplate them with suchness and equanimity, they will then apprehend a self within consciousness;”
If one attains the notion of a self within consciousness, one thereby attains the view of a self within consciousness;
if one attains the view of a self within consciousness, one thereby attains the view of a sentient being within consciousness;
if one attains the view of a sentient being within consciousness, one thereby finds no attainment of that view of a sentient being within consciousness.
When those sentient beings find nothing to be apprehended within consciousness, then those sentient beings themselves are also unapprehendable.

If there were any characteristic of apprehension that could be established regarding phenomena, then that characteristic of apprehension would have a basis; therefore, one cannot achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there is another person who can, regarding the measure of form within form and the measure of suffering within suffering, observe them as they truly are with equanimity, then they find no self within form;
if they find no self within form, then they find no view of a self within form."
If, within form, one finds nothing to be apprehended as a self-view, then within form, one finds nothing to be apprehended as a sentient-being-view;
if, within form, one finds nothing to be apprehended as a sentient-being-view, then within form, that sentient-being-view is apprehended;
and when that sentient-being-view is apprehended within form, then that sentient-being is also apprehended.

If there were any characteristic of attainment regarding phenomena that could be established, then there would be a basis for that characteristic of attainment; consequently, one would be unable to achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If there is anyone who, regarding the measure of all that exists within consciousness and the measure of all that exists within suffering, is able to contemplate them with suchness and equanimity, then within consciousness they find no self;”
If one finds no self within consciousness, then one finds no view of a self within consciousness;
if one finds no view of a self within consciousness, then one finds no view of a sentient being within consciousness;
if one finds no view of a sentient being within consciousness, then one finds that the view of those sentient beings within consciousness is something that can be attained.
If, within consciousness, those sentient beings perceive anything as being obtainable, then those sentient beings themselves are also characterized by obtainability.

If the characteristic of obtainability could be established regarding any phenomenon, then that characteristic of obtainability would have a basis; therefore, one cannot achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a person cannot observe form as it truly and equally is, because they unrealistically differentiate its dimensions and waver in their doubt regarding them, they will then apprehend form within form;
and when they apprehend form within form, they will see an apprehension within form."
If one perceives the apprehension of form within form, one perceives the apprehension of a sentient being within form;
if one perceives the apprehension of a sentient being within form, one perceives the apprehension of all things within form;
and when there is the apprehension of all things, there is the non-apprehension of all things.

If there were any characteristic of attainment regarding phenomena that could be established, then there would be a basis for that characteristic of attainment; consequently, one would be unable to achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.

“Subhūti! If a person cannot observe feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly and equally are, because of unreal conceptualization regarding their measure and wavering due to doubt, they will then apprehend consciousness within consciousness;
if they apprehend consciousness within consciousness, they will then perceive an apprehension within consciousness.”
If within consciousness one perceives the attainment of consciousness, then one perceives the attainment of sentient beings within consciousness;
if within consciousness one perceives the attainment of sentient beings, then one perceives the attainment of all things within consciousness;
when one perceives the attainment of all things within consciousness, then there is the non-attainment of all things.

If there were any characteristic of attainment regarding phenomena that could be established, then there would be a basis for that characteristic of attainment; consequently, one would be unable to achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.
The Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom Revealing the Innate Nature Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom Revealing the Innate Nature Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Radiant Dharma, Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Weijing, et al., by Imperial Decree. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a person can contemplate, in accordance with reality and with equanimity, all portions of unreal conceptualization and all portions of wavering doubt regarding form, then they will find nothing to be apprehended as "form within form.
When they find nothing to be apprehended as "form within form," they then see that there is nothing to be apprehended as "form within form";
when they see that there is nothing to be apprehended as "form within form," they then find nothing to be apprehended as a "sentient being within form."
If sentient beings find nothing to be apprehended within form, then they find nothing at all within form;
when they find nothing at all within form, then they find everything.
If there were any characteristic of attainment regarding phenomena that could be established, then that characteristic of attainment would have a basis.
For this reason, one cannot achieve liberation within that Mahāyāna Dharma, let alone within the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles.

“Subhūti! If a person can contemplate with suchness and equanimity all portions of unreal conceptualization and portions of wavering doubt within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then they will find nothing to be apprehended as ‘consciousness within consciousness.
When nothing is apprehended as ‘consciousness within consciousness,’ then one sees that there is nothing to be apprehended within consciousness.”
If within consciousness one finds nothing to be apprehended regarding consciousness itself, then one finds no sentient beings within consciousness;
if one finds no sentient beings within consciousness, then one finds nothing at all within consciousness;
when nothing whatsoever is found within consciousness, then everything is found.

If there were any characteristic of attainment regarding phenomena that could be established, then there would be a basis for that characteristic of attainment; consequently, one would be unable to achieve liberation within the Mahāyāna, let alone within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, regarding all forms (*rūpa*), gives rise to grasping and attachment according to their verbal designations and acts accordingly, such a practitioner practices the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and likewise practices craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)."
If one engages in practice while seeking apart from existence, this is a failure to understand the characteristics within form.
"Subhūti, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

If a bodhisattva, within the various consciousnesses, gives rise to grasping and attachment according to verbal expressions and acts accordingly, such a practitioner is practicing the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and is likewise practicing craving for existence (bhavarāga).
If one acts while seeking something apart from existence, this is a failure to understand the characteristics within consciousness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, regarding all forms,
does not give rise to grasping or attachment following verbal expressions, but acts without functional activity.
This is not practicing the view of a self-identity, nor is it practicing craving for existence.
Being free from seeking after existence and having no further practice, this is the thorough understanding of the characteristics within form.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva, regarding these various consciousnesses, does not give rise to grasping or attachment following their verbal expressions, and practices without functional activity, this is not practicing the view of a self-identity, nor is it practicing craving for existence.”
To be free from seeking existence and to have no further activity— this is the thorough understanding of the characteristics within consciousness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
regarding all forms (*rūpa*), is able to embrace them by means of the three kinds of mental seeds as conditions, this is called the purification of phenomena."
What are the three?
First, the seed of the mind of faith and understanding; second, the seed of the mind of weary detachment; third, the seed of the indestructible mind. "Subhūti!..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, within all forms of consciousness, is able to fully possess the three kinds of causal conditions for the seeds of the mind and thereby embrace them, this constitutes pure phenomena.
What are these three?
First, the seed of the mind of faith and understanding; second, the seed of the mind of weary detachment; third, the seed of the indestructible mind. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to three kinds of mind regarding all forms.
What are these three?
First, a mind free from grasping; second, a mind free from conjunction; third, a pure mind.

Therefore, Subhūti, regarding that form, whether the mind arises or does not arise, whether it arises extensively or arises equally, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should in all cases observe it with reality as it is and with equanimity.
Because they are able to contemplate with such equanimity, these bodhisattvas swiftly realize the fruit of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Subhūti!..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within all forms of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to three kinds of mind.
What are these three?
First, a mind free from grasping; second, a mind free from conjunction;
third, a pure mind. Therefore, Subhūti!

Regarding that consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, in accordance with reality, observe with equanimity whether the mind arises or does not arise, whether it arises extensively or arises equally.
Because they are able to contemplate with such equanimity, these bodhisattvas swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives existence or non-existence within all forms, it should be known that this bodhisattva does not possess true knowledge and understanding. "Subhūti!..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives existence or non-existence within these various consciousnesses, it should be known that this bodhisattva does not possess true knowledge and understanding.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the thought of wishing to abide within the realm of equality, when that mind seeks liberation from form, the mind immediately wavers and fluctuates within form; it moves and moves extensively."
For this reason, it should be known that this bodhisattva finds liberation difficult to attain.
Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to the thought desiring to abide within the realm of equality, when that mind seeks liberation from consciousness, the mind immediately wavers and shifts within consciousness, moving and moving pervasively.
For this reason, it should be known that this bodhisattva finds liberation difficult. Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the thought of wishing to abide within the realm of equality, and when that mind seeks liberation from form, if within that [mind] regarding form there is neither attachment nor non-attachment, for this reason, it should be known that this bodhisattva has well attained liberation.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the thought of wishing to abide within the realm of equality, and when that mind seeks liberation from consciousness, if within consciousness the mind is neither attached nor unattached—by virtue of this, one should know that this bodhisattva has well attained liberation.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes the dharma of signlessness within all forms, suffering ceases of its own accord and all signs become tranquil."
Because foolish ordinary beings cannot understand form as it truly is, they give rise to grasping and attachment toward form, which presently functions to obscure them.

Since they have given rise to a mind of grasping toward form and are presently obscured, they are unable to achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, due to such causes of grasping and obscuration, they remain for a long time within the various realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, undergoing the suffering of birth and death in an endless cycle of transmigration.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this; even so for the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness;

the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness; the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness; the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness; the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness; and the mind, phenomena, and mind-consciousness—all are likewise without intrinsic nature, having only a provisional nature, and no real nature.”

“Subhūti! Thus, the mental consciousness evolves in relation to the three natures; because foolish ordinary beings cannot understand consciousness as it truly is, they give rise to grasping and attachment toward consciousness and the like, which manifests as a veiling obscuration.”

Because they give rise to a mind of grasping toward consciousness and become obscured by it, they are unable to achieve liberation even within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, due to such causes of grasping and obscuration, they remain for a long time within the various realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, undergoing the suffering of birth and death in an endless cycle of transmigration.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! In this way, form (rūpa) evolves within the three natures (trisvabhāva). If a wise person understands this as it truly is, they will not give rise to grasping or attachment toward form, nor will it manifest and evolve; their mind will become clear and enlightened."

Because they do not give rise to grasping or attachment toward form and their minds have become clear and enlightened, they are able to achieve liberation within the Mahāyāna teachings, let alone within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, because they do not give rise to such grasping and attachment and their minds are thus opened and clarified, they do not spend a long time within those realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, seeking out the sufferings of birth and death.
When one finds nothing to be apprehended in form (*rūpa*), form is then everything, and there is no longer any illumination or manifestation;
once form is no longer illuminated, one realizes the equality of the nature of form (*rūpadharmasamatā*) as it truly is, and this Bodhisattva swiftly attains the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva investigates within all forms of consciousness and finds nothing to be apprehended in consciousness, then consciousness is everything, and there is no longer any illumination or manifestation.”

Once consciousness has ceased its illumination, one realizes the equality of the dharmas of consciousness as they truly are; such a bodhisattva swiftly attains the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Seeking, one finds no distinct phenomena; In the realm of objects, there is no reflecting mind.
When wisdom realizes the nature of dharmas, This is precisely the attainment of Bodhi."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands the dharma of non-substantiality within form, they will fulfill the cultivation of form within form, yet remain unmoved within the realm of form; such a bodhisattva will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands the dharma of the absence of intrinsic nature within consciousness, they will fulfill the cultivation of consciousness within consciousness, yet remain unmoved within the dharma-realm; such a bodhisattva will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The wise one thoroughly understands the absence of intrinsic nature;
With all practices fully perfected, yet remaining unmoved within the dharma-realm, One immediately attains all-knowledge."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Within form there is no meaning, no phrasing of meaning, and no great meaning. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can correctly and truly understand this as it is, that bodhisattva will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

Within consciousness there is no meaning, no phrasing, and no great meaning. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can correctly and truly understand this as it is, that bodhisattva will swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Without meaning and without the meaning of words, the Great Meaning is likewise so;
when Bodhisattvas understand this well, they swiftly attain the fruit of Bodhi."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all forms, should thoroughly understand the five kinds of greedy dharmas; having understood them, he should abandon them."
What are the five? First, craving through seeking; second, craving through pervasive seeking; third, craving through discrimination; fourth, craving; and fifth, great craving.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within all forms of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand the five kinds of craving; having understood them, he should abandon them.”
What are the five? First, craving for seeking; second, craving for pervasive seeking; third, craving for discrimination; fourth, craving; fifth, great craving.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within all forms (*rūpa*), can abandon these five attachments, they will find nothing to be apprehended regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of forms.
When the intrinsic nature of forms is not apprehended, then even form within form is not apprehended.”
When form within form is not apprehended, then form within form is apprehended;
when form within form is apprehended, then that very form within form is not apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is something apprehended or nothing apprehended among all forms, one completely transcends all categories of form; thus, one is able to renounce [the world] and achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can relinquish these five attachments within all forms of consciousness, they will find that the intrinsic nature of all consciousness is unobtainable.”
When the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is also unapprehendable;
when consciousness within consciousness is unapprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is apprehended;
and when consciousness within consciousness is apprehended, then that very consciousness within consciousness is unapprehendable.

Because of this, whether there is something apprehended or nothing apprehended within the various consciousnesses, one completely transcends all types of consciousness; thus, one is able to emerge from them and achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all forms (rūpa), should thoroughly understand five kinds of phenomena of aversion; having understood them, he should abandon them."
What are the five? First, anger through discursive thought; second, pervasive anger through discursive thought; third, anger through analytical investigation; fourth, anger; and fifth, great anger.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within all forms of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand the five kinds of dharmas of aversion; having understood them, he should abandon them.”
What are the five? First, anger through discursive thought; second, pervasive anger through discursive thought; third, anger through analytical reflection; fourth, anger; and fifth, great anger.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, amidst all forms,
is able to abandon these five types of anger, then— ”
One does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of forms;
when the intrinsic nature of forms is not apprehended, one does not apprehend form within form;
when form within form is not apprehended, one then apprehends form within form.
If, within form, there were anything of form to be apprehended, then that very form within form would be non-apprehensible.

Because it is thus, whether there is apprehension or non-apprehension regarding all forms, one completely transcends all categories of form; thereby, one is able to emerge and achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can abandon these five kinds of anger regarding all forms of consciousness, they will find nothing to be apprehended within the intrinsic nature of those consciousnesses.”
When the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is also unapprehendable;
when consciousness within consciousness is unapprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is apprehendable;
and when consciousness within consciousness is apprehendable, then that very consciousness within consciousness is unapprehendable.

Because of this, whether there is something apprehended or nothing apprehended within the various consciousnesses, one completely transcends all categories of consciousness; thus, one is able to emerge [from saṃsāra] and achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all forms (rūpa), should thoroughly understand five kinds of deluded states; having understood them, he should abandon them."

What are the five? First, the delusion of agitation; second, the delusion of the signs of agitation; third, the delusion of the absence of the signs of agitation; fourth, delusion; and fifth, great delusion.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all forms of consciousness, should thoroughly understand five kinds of deluded dharmas; having understood them, he should abandon them.”
What are these five?
First, the delusion of agitation; second, the delusion of the signs of agitation; third, the delusion of the absence of the signs of agitation; fourth, delusion; and fifth, great delusion.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to relinquish these five delusions regarding all forms (*rūpa*), they will find nothing to be apprehended in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of forms.
When the intrinsic nature of forms is not apprehended, then even form within form is not apprehended.”
When form within form is not apprehended, it is precisely within form that form is apprehended;
if form within form were apprehended, it would be precisely within that form that form is not apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is anything apprehended or nothing apprehended among all forms, one completely transcends all categories of form and is thus able to escape, accomplishing the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can abandon these five delusions regarding all forms of consciousness, they will find nothing to be apprehended in the intrinsic nature of those consciousnesses.”
When the self-nature of consciousness is not apprehended, then consciousness within consciousness is also not apprehended;
when consciousness within consciousness is not apprehended, then consciousness within consciousness is apprehended;
and when consciousness within consciousness is apprehended, then that very consciousness within consciousness is not apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is something apprehended or nothing apprehended within the various consciousnesses, one completely transcends all categories of consciousness; thus, one is able to emerge [from saṃsāra] and achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all forms (*rūpa*), should thoroughly understand five kinds of conceit; having understood them, he should abandon them."
What are the five? First, pride of erudition; second, pride of superiority; third, overweening pride; fourth, pride; and fifth, great pride.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Within all forms of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand the five kinds of conceit; having understood them, he should abandon them.”
What are the five? First, pride of erudition; second, pride of superiority; third, overweening pride; fourth, pride; and fifth, great pride.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to relinquish these five types of pride regarding all forms (*rūpa*), they will find nothing to be apprehended in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those forms.
When the intrinsic nature of form is not apprehended, then even ‘form within form’ is not apprehended.”
When form within form is not apprehended, it is precisely within form that form is apprehended;
when form within form is apprehended, it is precisely within that form that form is not apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is anything apprehended or nothing apprehended among all forms, one completely transcends all categories of form and is thus able to emerge [from saṃsāra], accomplishing the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has abandoned these five types of pride regarding all forms of consciousness, they will find nothing to be apprehended in the intrinsic nature of those consciousnesses."
When the self-nature of consciousness is non-apprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is also non-apprehendable;
when consciousness within consciousness is non-apprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is apprehendable;
and when consciousness within consciousness is apprehendable, then that very consciousness within consciousness is non-apprehendable.

Because of this, whether there is apprehension or non-apprehension within the various consciousnesses, one completely transcends all categories of consciousness; thus, one is able to escape and achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa and others, Imperially Appointed Dharma Propagator, Grand Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Donated-Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Fahu, during the Zhaodao era; by imperial decree: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding the phenomena of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should thoroughly understand five kinds of views; having understood them, he should abandon them. What are these five?

First, the view of inversion regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viparyāsa-dṛṣṭi*); second, the view of existence (*astitva-dṛṣṭi*); third, the view of denial (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*); fourth, the view (*dṛṣṭi*); and fifth, the great view (*mahādṛṣṭi*).
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand five kinds of views; having understood them, he should abandon them.”
What are the five? First, the view of inversion by intrinsic nature; second, the view of existence; third, the view of denial; fourth, the view; and fifth, the great view.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), is able to relinquish these five views, they then find nothing to be apprehended regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of forms.
When the intrinsic nature of forms is not apprehended, then even form within form is not apprehended.
When form within form is not apprehended, then form within form is apprehended;
when form within form is apprehended, then that very form within form is not apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is anything apprehended or nothing apprehended among all forms, one completely transcends all categories of form and is thus able to attain liberation, accomplishing the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, is able to relinquish these five views, they then find nothing to be apprehended regarding the intrinsic nature of consciousness.”
When the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is also unapprehendable;
when consciousness within consciousness is unapprehendable, then consciousness within consciousness is apprehended;
and when consciousness within consciousness is apprehended, then that very consciousness within consciousness is unapprehendable.

Because of this, whether there is something apprehended or nothing apprehended within the various consciousnesses, one completely transcends all categories of consciousness; thus, one is able to escape and achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the category of form, should thoroughly understand five kinds of doubtful phenomena; having understood them, he should abandon them."
What are these five? First, doubt regarding the Dharma;
second, doubt regarding the suffering of the various realms of existence; third, doubt regarding the tranquility of the dharmas of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; fourth, doubt; and fifth, great doubt.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand five kinds of doubtful dharmas; having understood them, he should abandon them.”
What are the five? First, doubt regarding the Dharma;
second, doubt regarding the suffering of the various realms of existence; third, doubt regarding the tranquility of the dharmas of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; fourth, doubt; and fifth, great doubt.
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has abandoned these five doubts regarding the dharma of form, they will find nothing to be apprehended in the intrinsic nature of forms.
When the intrinsic nature of forms is not apprehended, then even ‘form within form’ is not apprehended.”
When form within form is not apprehended, it is precisely within form that form is apprehended;
if form within form were apprehended, then within that very form, form would not be apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is anything apprehended or nothing apprehended among all forms, one completely transcends all categories of form and is thus able to attain liberation, accomplishing the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has abandoned these five doubts regarding the phenomenon of consciousness, they will find nothing to be apprehended in the intrinsic nature of consciousness.”
When the self-nature of consciousness is not apprehended, then even the consciousness within consciousness is not apprehended;
when the consciousness within consciousness is not apprehended, then the consciousness within consciousness is apprehended;
and when the consciousness within consciousness is apprehended, then that very consciousness within consciousness is not apprehended.

Because of this, whether there is something apprehended or nothing apprehended within the various consciousnesses, one completely transcends all categories of consciousness; thus, one is able to depart [from saṃsāra] and achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks anything within the dharma of form, or teaches the Dharma regarding form, or purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind regarding form—then, in that very form, he acts as he speaks, as he describes, and as he praises;

because he seeks in this way, teaches the Dharma in this way, and purifies his actions of body, speech, and mind in this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva instead seeks suffering within that form. You should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma incorrectly and is unable to purify his actions of body, speech, and mind."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, although seeking form, teaches the Dharma within form and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind within form, yet does not [seek] in form according to words, according to what is said, or according to what is praised;

because he seeks it not in such a way, teaches the Dharma not in such a way, and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind not in such a way—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can seek in form in this manner, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to teach the Dharma correctly and is able to purify the actions of body, speech, and mind within form.”
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks anything within the phenomenon of consciousness, or if they teach the Dharma regarding consciousness, or if they purify the actions of body, speech, and mind within consciousness—then it is only with respect to that consciousness as it is spoken of, as it is taught, and as it is praised.”

Because they seek in this manner, because they teach the Dharma in this manner, and because they purify their physical, verbal, and mental actions in this manner, yet that bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks suffering within that consciousness, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma incorrectly and is unable to purify their physical, verbal, and mental actions.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while seeking consciousness, teaches the Dharma within consciousness and purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind within consciousness;
yet, within that consciousness, they do not act as they speak, nor do they act as they praise;”

Because they do not seek in this way, do not teach the Dharma in this way, and do not purify the actions of body, speech, and mind in this way, it should be known that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks thus within consciousness, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly teach the Dharma and is able to purify the actions of body, speech, and mind within consciousness.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the thought of wishing to abide within the realm of equality, when they give rise to faith and understanding toward those material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they then apprehend duality within duality; that is to say, the material phenomenon that is the object of faith and understanding, and the material phenomenon that is the subject of faith and understanding."

If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva explains that which is to be resolved with faith within form according to what he himself resolves with faith, and explains that which he resolves with faith according to what is to be resolved with faith, it should be known that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva teaches the Dharma incorrectly regarding all forms.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because there is no distinguishing mark between the form that is the object of faith and understanding and the form that is the subject capable of faith and understanding.

Subhūti! If, within form, there were distinct characteristics between the object of faith and understanding and the subject of faith and understanding, then among the various faiths and understandings of all sentient beings, distinct characteristics would be visible and obtainable within the dharma of equality; in that case, the faith and understanding that is without an objective referent—such as that which is like a dream—could not be obtained.
Consequently, foolish ordinary beings conceive a view of reality regarding all forms; they do not accord with non-conceptual faith and understanding in accordance with the truth. "Subhūti!..."

If there is no turning toward conviction or understanding regarding form, then the various convictions and understandings of all sentient beings are entirely equal; within that which is believed and understood, no distinct characteristics can be seen or obtained, for it is like a dream—there is no object of perception in the conviction, yet something is attained.

Therefore, when foolish ordinary beings do not give rise to views of reality regarding various forms, they are in accord with non-conceptual faith and understanding according to the principle; thus, one should know that there is no difference between the form that is the object of faith and understanding and the form that possesses the capacity for faith and understanding.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should see it in this way; seeing it in this way, there is no distinct characteristic to be seen. Thus, within form (*rūpa*), whatever arises through the power of faithful understanding (*adhimukti*) is itself that which is faithfully understood. The meaning spoken of herein is clearly manifest.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, whatever they say constitutes correct discourse.

Because of this, one should know that within form (*rūpa*), the two dharmas of the subject that believes and understands (*adhimoktṛ*) and the object believed and understood (*adhimoktavya*) are conjoined; there is no object apart from the subject, yet it is not that the object does not exist.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first contemplate the perception of form that is capable of faith and understanding as it truly is; next, they likewise contemplate the two perceptions of form as they truly are. Having contemplated in this way, they find nothing at all to be apprehended within any form whatsoever.
When all forms (*rūpa*) are non-apprehendable, one apprehends movement and agitation within form;
when there is apprehension of movement and agitation within form, one apprehends the characteristic of movement and agitation in form;
and when there is apprehension of the characteristic of movement and agitation in form, there is a gathering together of the phenomena (*dharma*) of movement and agitation in form.
Because the phenomena of form’s agitation and disturbance have an accumulation, within that very form there is no accumulation of the phenomena of non-agitation and equality.

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not aggregate all the phenomena of agitation and non-agitation within such form as previously described, they will not rely upon those phenomena of agitation or the phenomena of non-agitation and equality within form; they shall instead cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly achieve the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to achieve such thorough awakening regarding all forms, whatever they say is correct speech. "Subhūti!..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to the thought of wishing to abide within the realm of equality, when they give rise to faith and understanding toward those phenomena of consciousness, they immediately apprehend two things within that duality: namely, the consciousness that is the object of faith and understanding, and the consciousness that is the subject of faith and understanding.

If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding consciousness, explains what he has resolved upon according to his faith, and explains his faith according to what he has resolved upon, it should be known that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva teaches the Dharma incorrectly regarding all forms of consciousness.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because there is no difference between the consciousness that cognizes what is believed and understood and the consciousness that is capable of believing and understanding.

Subhūti! If, within consciousness, there were distinct characteristics between the object of faith and understanding and the subject of faith and understanding, then among the various faiths and understandings of all sentient beings, distinct characteristics would be visible and obtainable within the dharma of equality; in that case, the faith and understanding that is without an objective referent—such as that found in dreams—would not be obtainable.

For this reason, foolish ordinary beings give rise to views of substantiality regarding the various consciousnesses; they do not accord with non-conceptual faith and understanding in accordance with reality. Subhūti!

If there is no turning toward any object of faith or understanding within consciousness, then the various faiths and understandings of all sentient beings are entirely equal; within that which is believed and understood, no distinct characteristics can be seen or obtained, just as in a dream, where there is no objective referent for faith or understanding, yet something is perceived.

Therefore, when foolish ordinary beings do not give rise to the view of reality regarding these various consciousnesses, they are in accord with non-conceptual faith and understanding according to the principle; for this reason, one should know that the consciousness which is capable of faith and understanding and the consciousness which is the object of faith and understanding have no distinct characteristics.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive it in this way; those who perceive it thus see no distinct characteristics whatsoever. Thus, within consciousness, whatever arises according to one's capacity for faith and understanding is itself that which is understood. The meaning explained herein is clear and manifest.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, whatever they say constitutes correct discourse.

Because of this, one should know that within consciousness, the two dharmas of the subject (the one who believes and understands) and the object (that which is believed and understood) are conjoined; there is no object apart from the subject, yet it is not that they do not exist.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first contemplate the conceptualization of consciousness that is capable of faith and understanding as it truly is; next, they likewise contemplate the two types of conceptualization of consciousness as they truly are. Having contemplated in this way, they find nothing at all to be apprehended within any consciousness.
When nothing is apprehended within any consciousness, there is the apprehension of movement and agitation within consciousness;
when there is the apprehension of movement and agitation within consciousness, there is the apprehension of the marks of the movement and agitation of consciousness.
When the signs of the agitation of consciousness are apprehended, there is a gathering of the phenomena of the agitation of consciousness;
because the phenomena of the agitation of consciousness are gathered, within that very consciousness, the phenomena of the equality of non-agitation are gathered.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not aggregate all the phenomena of agitation and non-agitation within such consciousness as previously described, they will, by relying on that very consciousness which is devoid of those phenomena of agitation and the phenomena of equanimity toward non-agitation, cultivate and accumulate all the Buddha-dharmas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and swiftly achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to thus skillfully awaken regarding all consciousnesses, whatever they say constitutes correct speech.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the category of form-dharmas, should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the dharma of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). What are these five?

First, the loving-kindness that embraces the true Dharma; second, the loving-kindness that embraces all worldly pleasures; third, the loving-kindness that embraces the supreme, wondrous bliss that transcends the world; fourth, loving-kindness; and fifth, great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the dharma of loving-kindness.”
What are these five?

First, the compassion that embraces the true Dharma; second, the compassion that embraces all worldly happiness; third, the compassion that embraces supramundane, sublime, and wondrous happiness; fourth, compassion; and fifth, great compassion.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are five aspects for practicing the dharma of compassion (*karuṇā*)."

What are these five? First, compassion free from attachment; second, compassion for those who are united; third, compassion for those who are separated; fourth, compassion; and fifth, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the dharma of compassion.”

What are these five? First, compassion free from attachment; second, compassion for those who are united; third, compassion for those who are separated; fourth, compassion; and fifth, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the dharma of joy."
What are these five?

First, the joy of sympathetic appreciation that upholds the purity of the True Dharma without impairment; second, the joy of sympathetic appreciation that upholds all worldly pleasures without impairment; third, the joy of sympathetic appreciation that upholds the sublime supramundane bliss without impairment; fourth, joy; and fifth, great joy.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the phenomenon of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects in which they practice the dharma of joy.”
What are these five?

First, the joy of sympathetic appreciation and acceptance that is pure and indestructible regarding the True Dharma; second, the joy of sympathetic appreciation and acceptance that is indestructible regarding all worldly pleasures; third, the joy of sympathetic appreciation and acceptance that is indestructible regarding the sublime supramundane bliss; fourth, joy; and fifth, great joy.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are five aspects for practicing the dharma of equanimity (*upekṣā*)."

What are the five? First, the relinquishment that eliminates all wrong views and various defilements; second, the relinquishment that distances one from all faults and eliminates various defilements; third, the relinquishment that gathers all merits and eliminates various defilements; fourth, relinquishment; and fifth, great relinquishment.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects in which they practice the dharma of equanimity.”
What are these five?

First, equanimity that eliminates all incorrect views and various defilements; second, equanimity that distances itself from all faults and eliminates various defilements; third, equanimity that gathers all meritorious qualities and eliminates various defilements; fourth, equanimity; and fifth, great equanimity.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that within the category of form (rūpa-dharma), there are five aspects in which one practices the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā)."
What are the five?
First, the gift of the vow; second, the gift of wealth and fearlessness; third, the gift of the Dharma; fourth, the gift; and fifth, the great gift.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of giving.”
What are the five? First, the gift of aspiration; second, the gift of material wealth and fearlessness; third, the gift of Dharma; fourth, the gift; and fifth, the great gift.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (rūpa-dharma), should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā)."
What are these five?
First, the precept of benefiting sentient beings; second, the precept of meditative dharmas; third, the precept of untainted dharmas; fourth, the precept; and fifth, the great precept.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of ethical discipline.”

What are the five? First, the precept of benefiting sentient beings; second, the precept of the dharmas of meditative concentration; third, the precept of the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*); fourth, the precept; and fifth, the great precept.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)."
What are these five?
First, the patience of enduring enmity and harm; second, the patience of accepting suffering; third, the patience of discerning the Dharma; fourth, patience; and fifth, great patience.
“Subhūti! It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Within the phenomenon of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of patience.”

What are the five? First, the patience of enduring enmity and harm; second, the patience of accepting suffering with equanimity; third, the patience of discerning the Dharma; fourth, patience; and fifth, great patience.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that within the category of form (rūpa-dharma), there are five aspects in which they should practice the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
What are the five?

First, the diligence of explaining, reciting, and contemplating; second, the diligence of distancing oneself from all faults; third, the diligence of gathering all virtues; fourth, diligence; and fifth, great diligence.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects in which they practice the perfection of diligence.”
What are these five?

First, the diligence of explaining, reciting, and contemplating; second, the diligence of distancing oneself from all faults; third, the diligence of gathering all virtues; fourth, diligence; and fifth, great diligence.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (rūpa-dharma), should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
What are the five?

First, the concentration that skillfully understands without departing from words; second, the initially pure mundane concentration that skillfully departs from words; third, supramundane concentration; fourth, concentration; and fifth, great concentration.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they practice the perfection of meditative concentration.”
What are these five?

First, the concentration of skillfully understanding without departing from words; second, the concentration of initial purity that skillfully departs from words, which is mundane; third, supramundane concentration; fourth, concentration; and fifth, great concentration.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (rūpa-dharma), should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) by thoroughly understanding five aspects."
What are these five?

First, the wisdom that relies on concentration not separated from words and letters; second, the wisdom that relies on the initially pure mundane concentration that is well-detached from words and letters; third, the wisdom that relies on supramundane concentration; fourth, wisdom; and fifth, great wisdom.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which they should practice the perfection of wisdom.”
What are these five?

First, the wisdom that relies upon concentration not separated from words and letters; second, the wisdom that relies upon the initially pure mundane concentration that is well-detached from words and letters; third, the wisdom that relies upon supramundane concentration; fourth, wisdom; and fifth, great wisdom.
