Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, by Imperial Decree: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are five aspects through which one should draw near to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). What are these five?
1. Approaching through listening and receiving; 2. Approaching through serving and practicing the teachings; 3. Approaching through cultivation and progress; 4. Approaching; 5. Great approaching.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which one should draw near to spiritual friends.”

What are the five? First, proximity through listening and receiving; second, proximity through serving, performing activities, and training in the Dharma; third, proximity through practicing and advancing; fourth, proximity; and fifth, great proximity.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva associates with spiritual friends in this manner, they are embraced by the skillful means of liberation; thus, they are able to generate great merit and swiftly attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five aspects through which one makes offerings to the Tathāgata within the category of form (rūpa-dharma).

What are the five? First, worship through various forms of praise, respect, and faith; second, worship through offerings of pure requisites and respect; third, worship through the practice of diligent progress; fourth, worship; and fifth, great worship.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Within the dharma of consciousness, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are five modes through which one makes offerings to the Tathāgata.”

What are the five? First, worship through various forms of praise, reverence, and offerings; second, worship through pure requisites and reverent offerings; third, worship through the practice of diligent progress; fourth, worship; and fifth, great worship.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can make offerings to the Tathāgata in this manner, in accordance with the principle of reality, they will receive the joint praise of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout boundless worlds; they will also receive the offerings and provisions of the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others; they will bring immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to maturity; they will adorn and purify Buddha-fields; and they will swiftly attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the perfection of generosity in accordance with reality within the category of form, if they cultivate giving with signs, they will also swiftly fulfill the perfection of generosity;
if they cultivate signless giving, they will also swiftly fulfill the perfection of generosity."
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the category of form, practice giving with signs or giving without signs? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing generosity within the category of form (*rūpadharma*) in order to seek liberation, perceives a liberation to be attained through generosity, or perceives a giver of generosity who attains liberation—if they practice in this manner, it should be known that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing generosity with signs (*sanimitta-dāna*) within the category of form.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing generosity within the category of form (rūpa-dharma) in order to seek liberation, finds no gift of liberation that can be obtained, nor any giver of liberation that can be obtained.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of form is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless giving within the category of form.
Subhūti, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, is able to accord with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in accordance with reality, whether they practice giving with signs (sanimitta-dāna), they will swiftly fulfill the perfection of giving;
or if they practice signless giving (animitta-dāna), they will likewise swiftly fulfill the perfection of giving.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice giving with signs or giving without signs within the dharma of consciousness? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing generosity within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, perceives a liberation through which generosity can be obtained, or perceives a giver of generosity who can effect liberation;
one should know that such a practitioner is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing generosity with signs (*nimitta*) within the dharma of consciousness.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing generosity within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, finds that there is no gift of liberation to be obtained, nor any giver of liberation to be obtained.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless giving within the dharma of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accord with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) in accordance with reality regarding the phenomena of form (*rūpa*), whether they practice ethical discipline with signs (*sanimitta*) or practice ethical discipline without signs (*animitta*),
they will swiftly bring the perfection of ethical discipline to fulfillment.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of form, cultivate the observance of precepts with signs or the observance of precepts without signs? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing the precepts within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*) to seek liberation, perceives that there is liberation to be attained through the precepts, or perceives that there is a precept that can effect liberation, then it should be known that such a practitioner is cultivating the precepts with signs (*sanimitta*) regarding form.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing and maintaining the precepts within the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*) in order to seek liberation, finds no liberation or maintained precept that can be apprehended, and finds no one who maintains the precepts capable of attaining liberation.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of form is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this way should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the precepts of signlessness within the dharma of form.
Subhūti, it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, is able to accord with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) in accordance with reality, if they practice ethical discipline with signs (sa-nimitta), they will also swiftly fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline;
if they practice ethical discipline without signs (a-nimitta), they will also swiftly fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, cultivate the observance of precepts with signs or the observance of precepts without signs? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing and maintaining the precepts to seek liberation within the dharma of consciousness, perceives that there is liberation to be attained through the maintenance of precepts, or perceives that there is a maintainer of precepts who can achieve liberation—if they practice in this manner, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the maintenance of precepts with signs (*nimitta*) within the dharma of consciousness.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing and maintaining the precepts within the dharma of consciousness in order to seek liberation, finds that there is no liberation or maintenance of precepts to be obtained, and no one who maintains the precepts to be found as the liberator.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the precepts of signlessness within the dharma of consciousness. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accord with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) in accordance with reality regarding the phenomenon of form (*rūpa*),
whether they practice patience that possesses signs (*sanimitta*) or practice patience that is signless (*animitta*), they will also swiftly fulfill the perfection of patience.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of form, cultivate patience with signs or patience without signs? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing patience within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*) in order to seek liberation, perceives a liberation through patience that can be attained, or perceives a patience capable of liberating that can be attained—if they practice in this manner, it should be known that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing patience with signs (*sanimitta-kṣānti*) within the category of form.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing patience within the category of form-dharmas in order to seek liberation, finds no patience that can be liberated, nor does he find any one who can liberate that patience.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of form is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when one contemplates all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the patience of signlessness (*animitta-kṣānti*) within the dharma of form (*rūpa*).
Subhūti, it is likewise for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, is able to accord with the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in accordance with reality,
whether they cultivate patience with signs (sanimitta) or cultivate patience without signs (animitta), they will swiftly fulfill the perfection of patience.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate patience with signs or patience without signs regarding the dharma of consciousness? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing patience within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, perceives a liberation through patience that can be attained, or perceives a patience capable of liberating that can be attained—then it should be known that such a practitioner is cultivating patience with signs within the dharma of consciousness.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing patience within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, finds no patience that can be liberated, nor any patience that can effect liberation.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the patience of signlessness within the dharma of consciousness. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accord with the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā) in accordance with reality regarding the phenomenon of form (rūpa), if they cultivate diligence with signs (sanimitta), they will swiftly fulfill the perfection of diligence;
if they cultivate signless diligence (animitta), they will likewise swiftly fulfill the perfection of diligence.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate either sign-possessing diligence or signless diligence within the dharma of form? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing diligence to seek liberation within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), perceives a liberation that can be attained through diligence, or perceives a liberating diligence that can be attained—if they practice in this manner, it should be known that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing diligence characterized by signs (*nimitta*) within the category of form.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing diligence to seek liberation within the category of form-dharmas, finds no diligence that can be liberated, nor any diligence that is capable of liberating.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of form is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this way should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless diligence within the category of form.
Subhūti, it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, is able to accord with the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) in accordance with reality, whether they cultivate diligence with signs (sanimitta-vīrya), they will swiftly fulfill the perfection of diligence;
or if they cultivate signless diligence (animitta-vīrya), they will likewise swiftly fulfill the perfection of diligence.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate either sign-associated diligence or signless diligence within the dharma of consciousness? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing diligence to seek liberation within the dharma of consciousness, perceives a liberation-diligence that can be attained or a liberating-diligence that can be attained, then one should know that such a practitioner is cultivating diligence with signs (*nimitta*) regarding the dharma of consciousness.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, no diligence that effects liberation can be found, nor can any diligence that is capable of effecting liberation be found.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless diligence within the dharma of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accord with the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) in accordance with reality regarding the category of form (rūpadharma), whether they cultivate meditative concentration with signs (sanimitta-dhyāna) or cultivate signless meditative concentration (animitta-dhyāna),
they will swiftly bring the perfection of meditative concentration to full completion.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate either the dhyāna with signs or the dhyāna without signs within the category of form? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing meditative concentration within the category of form (*rūpadharma*) to seek liberation, perceives a meditative concentration that is liberated, or perceives a meditative concentration that is capable of liberating, one should know that such a practitioner is cultivating meditative concentration with signs (*nimitta*) within the category of form.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing meditative concentration within the category of form-dharmas to seek liberation, finds no meditative concentration that is liberated and finds no meditative concentration that is capable of liberating.
Why is this? It is because the intrinsic nature of form is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, even when observing all Tathāgatas, they are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this way should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless dhyāna-concentration within the category of form (*rūpa*).
Subhūti, it is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, is able to accord with the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) in accordance with reality, if they cultivate meditative concentration with signs (sanimitta-dhyāna), they will also swiftly fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration;
if they cultivate signless meditative concentration (animitta-dhyāna), they will likewise swiftly fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of consciousness, cultivate meditative concentration with signs or meditative concentration without signs? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing dhyāna-concentration within the phenomenon of consciousness to seek liberation, perceives a dhyāna-concentration that is liberated and perceives a dhyāna-concentration that is capable of liberating, one should know that such a practitioner is cultivating dhyāna-concentration with signs (*sanimitta*) within the phenomenon of consciousness.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing meditative concentration within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, finds no meditative concentration that can be liberated, nor any meditative concentration that is capable of liberating.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of consciousness is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless meditative concentration within the dharma of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the category of form-dharmas, is able to accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) according to reality, whether they cultivate the conceptualized perfection of wisdom, they will swiftly fulfill the perfection of wisdom;
or if they cultivate the non-conceptualized perfection of wisdom, they will likewise swiftly fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the dharma of form,
cultivate prajñā with signs or prajñā without signs?

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing prajñā within the dharma of form (rūpa) to seek liberation, perceives a prajñā that is liberated, or perceives a prajñā that is capable of liberating, then one should know that such a practitioner is cultivating prajñā with signs (sanimitta-prajñā) regarding the dharma of form.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing prajñā within the dharma of form (rūpa) to seek liberation, finds that no liberating prajñā can be apprehended and no prajñā that performs liberation can be apprehended.
Why is this? It is because the intrinsic nature of form is unapprehendable, and its fundamental nature is unapprehendable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unapprehendable, for their fundamental nature is unapprehendable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless prajñā within the dharma of form.
Subhūti, it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the phenomenon of consciousness, is able to accord with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) according to reality, whether they cultivate the conceptualized perfection of wisdom, they will swiftly fulfill the perfection of wisdom;
or if they cultivate the non-conceptualized perfection of wisdom, they will likewise swiftly fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate prajñā with signs or prajñā without signs within the dharma of consciousness? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing *prajñā* within the dharma of consciousness (*vijñāna*) to seek liberation, perceives a *prajñā* that is liberated and perceives a *prajñā* that is capable of liberating, one should know that such a practitioner is cultivating *prajñā* with signs (*sanimitta*) within the dharma of consciousness.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing prajñā within the dharma of consciousness to seek liberation, finds no prajñā that is liberated and no prajñā that is capable of liberating.
Why is this? It is because the self-nature of consciousness is unattainable, and its fundamental nature is unattainable;
likewise, when observing all Tathāgatas, they too are unattainable, for their fundamental nature is unattainable.
One who practices in this manner should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing signless prajñā within the dharma of consciousness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the category of form (*rūpa*), should thoroughly understand the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Subhūti, what is the emptiness samādhi within form?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the emptiness of non-existence within form; the emptiness of nature is likewise so, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is likewise so.
Regarding all objects of focus, one should abide in one-pointedness of mind; this is precisely what is called the samādhi of emptiness within form.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding form, thus understands the emptiness samādhi as it truly is, it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand the signless samādhi within the category of form. Subhūti,"
What is the signless samādhi within form?
It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the emptiness of non-existence within form, as well as the emptiness of nature and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

If one can act in this way, all mental engagements (manasikāra) will cease; one will then contemplate the characteristic of non-existence within form, and likewise the characteristic of existence, as well as the characteristics of both existence and non-existence.

In this way, one attains the state where the characteristic of non-existence is free from following after consciousness; likewise, the characteristic of existence is also free from following after consciousness. Furthermore, the characteristics of both existence and non-existence are likewise free from following after consciousness.
Therefore, one is able to dwell securely in one-pointedness of mind; this is precisely the signless samādhi within form. "Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding form, thus understands the signless samādhi as it truly is, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly understand the wishless samādhi within the category of form. Subhūti,..."
What is the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) regarding form?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*) regarding form, they then contemplate the characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) within form, without following after the characteristics of the objective referent (*ālambana-nimitta*). This applies likewise to the characteristic of having intrinsic nature; likewise to the characteristic of both having and lacking intrinsic nature—in each case, they do not follow after the characteristics of the objective referent. Thus, they are able to abide in one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*); this is precisely what constitutes the concentration of wishlessness regarding form.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding form, thus understands the wishless samādhi as it truly is, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (rūpa-dharma), should understand that there are three meanings regarding the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-anityatā).
What are these three?
First, the meaning of unreality; second, the meaning of disintegration; and third, the meaning of being with or without defilement. "Subhūti!..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so; a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should understand that there are three meanings by which all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
regarding the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are three meanings by which all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering."
What are these three?
First, the meaning of non-attachment; second, the meaning of the three kinds of characteristics; and third, the meaning of continuity. "Subhūti!..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are three meanings by which all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), should understand that there are three meanings of the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*)."
What are these three?

First, the meaning of selflessness regarding the absence of intrinsic nature; second, the meaning of selflessness regarding both the presence and absence of intrinsic nature; and third, the meaning of selflessness regarding original purity.

“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are three meanings by which all phenomena are without self.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Regarding the phenomenon of form (*rūpa*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are three kinds of meanings concerning the tranquility of nirvāṇa."
What are these three?

First, the meaning of ultimate quiescence as the absence of intrinsic nature within form; second, the meaning of quiescence as both the presence and absence of intrinsic nature; and third, the meaning of quiescence as the primordial purity of intrinsic nature.
“Subhūti! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that there are three meanings of the quiescence of nirvāṇa.”

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the venerable Subhūti, and all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as all the world with its gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom for the Awakening of Self-Nature Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
